newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's ex-bodyguard breaks into politics.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's ex-bodyguard breaks into politics.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's burly ex-bodyguard, who has promised to reveal the secrets of the Kremlin, broke into politics on Monday by winning a seat in the Russian parliament.

Alexander Korzhakov, a former close friend who is now one of Yeltsin's fiercest opponents, won 26 percent of Sunday's vote in the central Russian city of Tula, according to preliminary results announced by the local electoral commission.
The former KGB major took a leaf out of Yeltsin's book for his aggressive campaign, bringing rock and pop stars to the sleepy town and overwhelming the media with his advertising.
He emerged more than nine points clear of his nearest rival, local politician Eduard Pashchenko, in an election bizarre even by the standards of Russia's colourful political scene.

Chess champion Anatoly Karpov was just behind in third place and Nikolai Novikov, a businessman who ran his campaign from a prison cell while awaiting trial for extortion, was fourth. He denies the extortion charges.
The other six candidates in the field were far behind.

Some analysts predict that Korzhakov will use the platform of the Duma and the immunity from prosecution enjoyed by deputies to step up his fight against Yeltsin, who sacked him and other Kremlin hawks in June.
A close friend of Yeltsin for 10 years, Korzhakov has presented himself as a victim of a Kremlin plot and pledged to unveil "compromising material" against the establishment.
"I think he has enough material to make trouble for many Russian politicans," said Andrei Piontkovsky, of the Moscow Centre for Strategic Studies.

Last May Korzhakov, who dramatically bolstered the Kremlin guard, said he wanted the presidential election to be postponed, putting him on collision course with liberal Anatoly Chubais, then effective head of Yeltsin's campaign.
Chubais, now Kremlin chief of staff, has been called a regent by Korzhakov who says he has assumed huge powers since Yeltsin fell ill with heart problems in June.

Yeltsin dismissed Korzhakov before July's presidential runoff, which he won, and ordered an inquiry into the general's activities. Korzhakov fought back by going to court and accusing Yeltsin of defamation. There has been no decision yet.

Russia's television channels, loyal to Yeltsin, attacked Korzhakov in a bid to put the voters off, but the residents of Tula showed the nationwide tendency to favour the candidate seen to carry political weight in the capital.

Korzhakov made up for a lack of charisma by promising to use his inside knowledge of the Kremlin to help Tula, a former defence industry centre suffering from the end of the Cold War and a post-communist economic slump.
Voters turned out for his pre-election rallies eager to hear some Kremlin gossip, but Korzhakov remained tight-lipped, saying he would only spill the beans once he was elected.
The Tula seat fell vacant when popular general Alexander Lebed was brought into the Kremlin last June as Yeltsin's security chief.
Lebed, sacked in October, first backed Korzhakov in the election race but then distanced himself from the 47-year-old, calling him "a mere bodyguard".
Turnout on Sunday was 43 percent of the 500,000-strong electorate, a high figure for an impoverished town where people are more concerned with survival than with politics.
